newsitem.title: USA: Tepid dlr/yen trade reaction showcases dollar/mark.
newsitem.headline: Tepid dlr/yen trade reaction showcases dollar/mark.

text.p: In an odd turn of events on Friday, news the U.S. posted another small import-export gap propelled the dollar to a 31-month high against the mark, leaving dollar/yen on the sidelines.

Traders typically direct their enthusiasm over a narrowing U.S. trade deficit at dollar/yen, but given recent yen- supportive jawboning from Japan, dollar/mark's upside path has been comparatively unobstructed.
Dollar/mark is holding a course plotted by officials on both side of the Atlantic, while Japan has successfully diverted wind from dollar/yen's sails, analysts said.
"There still is alot of uneasiness about the Japanese attitude towards yen weakness," said Ron Leven, currency strategist at J.P. Morgan Securities.
"Whereas in dollar/mark, the general perception is that at the central banks, both here and in Europe, there is universal applause towards dollar appreciation versus Europe."
The dollar rose to a high of 1.6190 marks on Friday, after news the U.S. international trade deficit rose 4.9 percent to $8.4 billion in November.
Yet, although the dollar clung to support at 117 yen after the trade data, it failed to recapture its 45-month peak of 117.48 set on Wednesday.

The trade gap was substantially narrower than the $9.8 billion forecast. Coming on the heels of a small $8.01 billion deficit in October, economists applauded the number, which showed another export gain, despite dollar strength and weak demand from economies overseas.
The dollar's rally versus the mark has come amid uncertainty ahead of European Economic and Monetary Union.

There is also speculation many European countries desire weaker currencies to gain competitive advantange for their exports after they fix exchange rates prior to a planned European currency union in 1999.
This has fueled talk that some European central banks have recently sold their currencies and bought dollars.

Since the beginning of the year, dollar/yen has been buffeted by comments from Japanese cabinet members, the most recent being Finance Minister Hiroshi Mitsuzuka on Thursday, who warned about excessive speculation against the yen.
But while the Bank of Japan has so far failed to follow up threats with open intervention, rumors of BOJ sales on Thursday was a disincentive to buy dollar/yen.

"I think the market is too interested in selling the deutschemark to take the yen seriously at this point, given the ambiguity," said David DeRosa, managing partner at Quadrangle Investments, a hedge fund.
"The mark move (on Friday) to a certain extent dragged dollar/yen up with it, but not as fast as ordinarily would be the case, because there have been large sellers of dollar/yen above 117.00."

From a technical standpoint, analysts said the dollar's rally against the yen has lost all momentum. The aggressive Japanese jawboning in the wake of the slump of the Nikkei 225 stock index below 20,000 last week, helped slow the advance.
On the other hand, the dollar's rally against the mark seems to be gaining strength, they said.
Japan's share market slide was exacerbated by budget belt-tightening proposals that could strangle Japan's already struggling economy.

While a weaker yen might help the Japanese economy export its way out of trouble, goverment officials are loath to tolerate further depreciation until the Nikkei stabilizes, fearing further flight by foreign investors might aggravate the downward spiral, analysts said.

"This is a Nikkei question, much less a dollar/yen question," said David Durrant, senior currency strategist at I.D.E.A. Inc. "The fact is they will continue to hold dollar/yen until the Nikkei finds its bottom."
